title: Triad shapes on three strings
summary: Tiny three-note voicings cover the entire fretboard and unlock chord melody.

steps.title: Why three-string triads?
steps.body:
Open-position chords are great for strumming but they're stuck in one place on the neck. Three-string triads -- one note per string on three adjacent strings -- are tiny, movable, and live everywhere. They're the foundation of chord melody, funk comping, and any time you need 'just enough chord' to imply harmony.

We'll learn the three inversions of C major on the highest three strings (G, B, E).

steps.title: Root position: C E G
steps.body: Bass note (C) on string 3, 3rd (E) on string 2, 5th (G) on string 1. The root is the lowest note, hence 'root position'.

steps.title: First inversion: E G C
steps.body: Same notes, different stacking. The 3rd is now on the bottom. Notice each note moved up one chord tone (C -> E, E -> G, G -> C).

steps.title: Second inversion: G C E
steps.body: The 5th is now on the bottom. Climb to the top of the neck for the highest voicing -- a great 'cap' for a chord melody arrangement.

steps.title: Make them minor
steps.body: To turn any of these into a minor triad, lower the 3rd by one fret. For root position (frets 5-5-3), the 3rd is on string 2 fret 5 -- drop it to fret 4 to get C minor (C Eb G). Try it for all three inversions; the muscle memory is identical to major minus one note.

steps.title: C minor, root position
steps.body: Same shape as major, with the 3rd lowered.

steps.title: Why this matters
steps.body:
Once you know all three inversions of major and minor on one string set, you can:
- comp a 12-bar blues without ever leaving frets 5-12,
- play chord melodies (the highest note of the inversion sings the melody),
- voice-lead between chords smoothly (move the closest note instead of leaping).

Next stop: applying these shapes everywhere via the CAGED system.
